content.content:
**Publication date:** November 3, 2026

**What Perplexity achieved:** Perplexity earned a FedRAMP "Class C" certification under the full, accelerated 20x process. It is the first such certification, and it is compliant with the FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026. The article describes Class C as the category most aligned with the old "moderate" level. Perplexity is "the first company to be certified under the full sped-up 20x process," per the article's deck.

**Class counts (per the article):**
- **Class A:** Seven certifications, a new entry-level type that began rolling out in August.
- **Class B:** Twelve 20x certifications in the pilot phase, comparable to the old "low" level.
- **Class C:** Perplexity's full certification, plus pilot Class C certifications for OpenAI's ChatGPT and Filevine, and about a dozen others.
- **Class D:** None yet, and no full Class B certifications have been issued either.

**AI products and certifications mentioned:**
- **Perplexity:** Full Class C certification.
- **OpenAI ChatGPT:** Class C pilot certification.
- **Google Gemini for Government:** Class B pilot certification.
- **Anthropic and Cisco:** Among nearly 100 products that have started the certification process. The article does not say they hold any certification yet.

**The 17-month timeline:** FedRAMP said it took "over 17 months from the announcement of the FedRAMP 20x initiative" to reach the first Class A certification. The article also notes that more than two years passed after the OMB memo requiring faster processes.

**Agencies that can use Perplexity:** The General Services Administration and the Department of Agriculture can now use the Perplexity Enterprise and API Platform. According to a company blog post, this brings "live web search and source-cited answers within its certified environment."

  HEADLINE: EU court adviser says AI chatbot answers can infringe press publishers' rights
  PUBLISHED: Reuters — Nov 3, 2026, 3:19 AM (as timestamped on the syndicating station, byline "BRUSSELS, Nov 3"); The IPKat — 3 November 2026, described in the post as "This morning"
  SOURCES:
  Reuters (via WTAQ) | https://wtaq.com/2026/11/03/googles-use-of-press-by-ai-chatbot-may-infringe-copyright-rules-eu-court-adviser-says/ | report
  The IPKat (Eleonora Rosati) | https://ipkitten.blogspot.com/2026/11/ag-szpunars-opinion-in-like-company-is.html | report (legal analysis)
  FACTS:
  - Reuters quotes Advocate General Maciej Szpunar: "When an LLM (large language model)-driven chatbot retrieves a publication from a press publisher's website, reuses that publication to generate an answer, and provides that answer to the user, the press publisher's right may be infringed in certain circumstances." Reuters says Gemini's answers fall under the publishers' right of reproduction when chatbots access publications "by unlawfully circumventing paywalls or other technical barriers, or when they reuse 'the form of expression of that publication in a recognisable manner'," and that copyright rules do not protect the "mere facts" reported by press publications, "only the specific form of expression."
  - Reuters reports Szpunar said using copyright-protected material to train LLMs is "freely permitted under the text and data mining exception," and that "there was no evidence that Google had used the Hungarian publisher's articles to train Gemini." The case pits Hungarian website operator Like Company against Google's Gemini before the CJEU. Reuters notes the court "follows the majority of its advisers' non-binding opinions" and "will rule in the coming months."
  - The IPKat says this is "the first referral to reach the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) regarding the interplay between copyright/related rights and Artificial Intelligence," that the Opinion runs to 240 paragraphs, and that the AG proposes the CJEU "declares inadmissible the questions regarding the training of the LLM in question (Google's Gemini)" while answering those on whether a chatbot's displayed responses may infringe press publishers' rights.
  - The IPKat reports the AG's reasoning that Article 15 of the DSM Directive "only concerns 'online uses' of a press publication" and that "LLM training is not a form of online use, thus rendering the right inapplicable"; that Article 4(1) DSM "is in principle applicable to LLM training"; but that "Article 4 of the DSM Directive does not apply" to a chatbot's use of a press publication in generating answers because that use "is not for the purpose of TDM." It quotes the AG that "An act of making available to the public of the press publication at issue occur if the form of expression in all or part of that publication is systematically recognisable."
  - The IPKat notes two further AI/copyright referrals are pending at the CJEU — Manchester United Fanatics Klub, C-806/26 and Mobilguru, C-829/26 — and that 3 November was also "the final day to submit responses to the European Commission's Public Consultation" on technology and copyright.
  - Reuters quotes a Google spokesperson: "European law's text and data mining exceptions are vital for Europe's competitiveness and AI development, and we acknowledge the Advocate General's opinion recognising that EU law permits AI training on publicly available information… Gemini learns linguistic patterns to create original outputs rather than replicating content, supported by extensive publisher controls." European Publishers Council executive director Angela Mills Wade is quoted: "Publishers should not have to choose between search visibility and protecting their rights."
  FLAGS: window-edge — the Opinion was delivered on the morning of 3 November in Luxembourg and Reuters' syndicated timestamp (3:19 AM, station local) and IPKat's "this morning" both point to publication shortly BEFORE the 11:50Z window start.   NBC4 Columbus (WCMH) | https://www.nbc4i.com/news/your-local-election-hq/columbus-area-communities-vote-on-data-center-issues-live-results/ | report
  FACTS:
  - Ballotpedia says voters in 10 states decided 41 ballot measures affecting local data centre policy on Nov. 3; a "yes" on 28 would limit development (17 would ban data centres — 12 above a size threshold, 5 all of them) and a "yes" on 13 would facilitate it. Ohio had 21, Illinois 7, Maine 4, Kansas 3; California, Florida, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota and Wisconsin one each.
  - Stateline reports that late Tuesday evening "33 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by voters or were leading in ongoing vote counts, according to the tracking website Data Centers on the Ballot," with roughly a dozen more measures in communities where totals had not been announced, and that "only one measure, in North Dakota, resulted in a victory for voters who supported the construction of data centers."
  - Fortune reports "at least 14 municipalities passing bans or other restrictions on data centers" in Ohio, where residents across 18 municipalities voted on 21 measures. In Trenton a ban passed 80% to 20%; in Perry more than 87% of voters approved requiring developers seeking tax breaks to give the village financial guarantees; in Wilmington around 80% of voters rejected rezoning across four separate referendums. Fortune says Ohio already has 125 local data centre moratoriums in place, ranks No. 5 among US states in number of data centre projects with more than 200 operational, and that per state data companies plan to invest up to $40 billion in AI infrastructure there by 2030.
  - NBC4 Columbus reports all five central Ohio communities voted to reject data centres, each with 100% of the unofficial vote counted: Grove City's Issue 28 requires a citizen referendum on developments of 50+ acres, more than 20 megawatts at peak capacity or more than 500,000 gallons of water per day; Pataskala, Sunbury and Granville each passed charter bans on data centres at or above 25 megawatts; Ashville voted to overturn its agreement with EdgeConneX (NBC4 notes overturning it "will not stop construction, which is already underway").
  - Ballotpedia notes six such measures were decided earlier in 2026 and in each case a majority favoured greater limits, including Canterbury, N.H. approving a ban 83.6% to 16.4% (March 10), Monterey Park, Calif. approving a ban 88.3% to 11.7% (June 2) and Nottingham, N.H. approving a one-year permitting moratorium 90.3% to 9.7% (Sept. 8). Two more votes follow: Clarksville, Ark. on Dec. 1 and Mandan, N.D. on Dec. 15.
  - Stateline cites a UMass Amherst poll published earlier this year finding "only 11% of Americans would support the construction of an AI data center in their community."
  FLAGS: (counts are unofficial/uncertified; CNBC's same-day tally says only "at least 10 communities approving bans or restrictions," which conflicts with Fortune's 14 and Stateline's 33 — attribute each number to its source)

HEADLINE: Voters approve data-centre bans and limits in nearly every local ballot measure nationwide
PUBLISHED: Ballotpedia News — November 3, 2026 at 8:27 PM; NBC4 Columbus — Posted Nov 3, 2026 / 07:30 PM EST, Updated Nov 4, 2026 / 12:32 AM EST; Fortune — November 4, 2026, 1:35 AM ET; Stateline — November 4, 2026
SOURCES:

Stateline | https://stateline.org/2026/11/04/voters-across-the-country-reject-data-centers/ | report
Fortune | https://fortune.com/2026/11/04/ohio-data-center-ballot-measures-midterm-elections/ | report
NBC4 Columbus (WCMH) | https://www.nbc4i.com/news/your-local-election-hq/columbus-area-communities-vote-on-data-center-issues-live-results/ | report
FACTS:
- Ballotpedia says voters in 10 states decided 41 ballot measures affecting local data centre policy on Nov. 3; a "yes" on 28 would limit development (17 would ban data centres — 12 above a size threshold, 5 all of them) and a "yes" on 13 would facilitate it. Ohio had 21, Illinois 7, Maine 4, Kansas 3; California, Florida, Nevada, New Jersey, North Dakota and Wisconsin one each.
- Stateline reports that late Tuesday evening "33 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by voters or were leading in ongoing vote counts, according to the tracking website Data Centers on the Ballot," with roughly a dozen more measures in communities where totals had not been announced, and that "only one measure, in North Dakota, resulted in a victory for voters who supported the construction of data centers."
- Fortune reports "at least 14 municipalities passing bans or other restrictions on data centers" in Ohio, where residents across 18 municipalities voted on 21 measures. In Trenton a ban passed 80% to 20%; in Perry more than 87% of voters approved requiring developers seeking tax breaks to give the village financial guarantees; in Wilmington around 80% of voters rejected rezoning across four separate referendums. Fortune says Ohio already has 125 local data centre moratoriums in place, ranks No. 5 among US states in number of data centre projects with more than 200 operational, and that per state data companies plan to invest up to $40 billion in AI infrastructure there by 2030.

- Ballotpedia notes six such measures were decided earlier in 2026 and in each case a majority favoured greater limits, including Canterbury, N.H. approving a ban 83.6% to 16.4% (March 10), Monterey Park, Calif. approving a ban 88.3% to 11.7% (June 2) and Nottingham, N.H. approving a one-year permitting moratorium 90.3% to 9.7% (Sept. 8). Two more votes follow: Clarksville, Ark. on Dec. 1 and Mandan, N.D. on Dec. 15.
- Stateline cites a UMass Amherst poll published earlier this year finding "only 11% of Americans would support the construction of an AI data center in their community."
FLAGS: (counts are unofficial/uncertified; CNBC's same-day tally says only "at least 10 communities approving bans or restrictions," which conflicts with Fortune's 14 and Stateline's 33 — attribute each number to its source)

Democrats' sweeping midterms victory marked a major rejection of Elon Musk and the artificial-intelligence industry, as a broad backlash against U.S. President Donald Trump and his tech allies put their political influence — and the debt-fueled data center buildout — under sharper scrutiny.
Musk, who spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms, funneled $224 million, or nearly half, into Texas alone, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records, only to see his favored candidates, Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott, trounced in a Democratic wave.

The defeats rattled markets overnight, sending SpaceX and Tesla shares lower, both of which have long flourished under Abbott's business-friendly. Meanwhile, broader tech stocks came under pressure as Democrats secured control of Congress.
Across the country, voters pushed back against billionaire influence and the growing power of technology companies, electing critics of the AI industry and approving restrictions on data centers fueling its expansion.
"We must get big money out of our politics, so no billionaire or trillionaire can buy our elections," Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico said in his victory speech, without naming Musk. "We must unrig this economic system that only benefits the top 1%."
J.C. Lintzenich, a visiting senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund, pointed to Musk's massive spending in Texas, telling CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday that the results were "clearly a rejection of the Elon Musk aspect that has found its way into the Trump orbit."

These operations rely heavily on state decisions regarding electricity, water, environmental permits, infrastructure, and tax incentives. Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned against generous corporate subsidies, and Musk himself — will wield significant influence over those decisions.
Hinojosa has called for a moratorium on new data centers, an end to industry tax breaks and requirements that developers cover their full electricity costs. In her victory speech Tuesday, she vowed to take power from the "powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state."
Republicans still control the Legislature, limiting Hinojosa's ability to overhaul state policy. But her administration could complicate Musk's expansion plans with a tougher approach to permitting and business incentives.

Gina Hinojosa, Democratic nominee for Texas Governor, is seen alongside Senate candidate James Talarico during a political rally ahead of Election Day in Houston, Saturday, Oct. 31, 2026.
Jason Fochtman | Houston Chronicle | Getty Images

Nationwide, Musk's America PAC spent nearly $87 million across 44 federal races, according to a CNBC analysis of FEC filings. By Wednesday morning, Republicans it backed had lost 29 contests and won just three, with 12 still uncalled. More than $80 million — or 93% of its spending — went toward races Republicans lost.

America PAC backed eight losing congressional candidates in 2024, and last year Musk spent over $20 million trying to elect a conservative in Wisconsin. Though Musk promised last year to spend "a lot less" on politics, he ultimately became the biggest known donor in the 2026 midterms.

In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted after attacking his support for data centers. Democrats spent nearly $28 million on advertisements criticizing data centers, according to AdImpact.
In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Sen. Darline Graham despite a late advertising push by Building the Future, a new data center industry super PAC that made Graham its first candidate to back. The group reserved $1.5 million in ads supporting Graham, while Andrews campaigned for a two-year moratorium on new data centers.
Nationwide, campaigns and outside groups spent $173 million on ads about data centers during the 2026 general election, with the ads almost entirely negative, according to AdImpact. Democratic advertisers accounted for $140 million of that spending. Voters also considered 41 local data center measures Tuesday, with at least 10 communities approving bans or restrictions .
The financial stakes are enormously high.
JPMorgan Asset Management estimates the AI infrastructure buildout could cost roughly $5 trillion through 2030, including about $2 trillion financed through investment-grade debt markets.

Voters across the country reject data centers • Stateline

Skip to main content

0:48

News Story

In local elections across the country, Americans voted overwhelmingly to restrict the buildout of data centers in their communities.

Late Tuesday evening, 33 ballot measures to restrict data centers were passed by voters or were leading in ongoing vote counts, according to the tracking website Data Centers on the Ballot . Roughly a dozen similar measures were on the ballot in communities where vote totals had not yet been announced.

The measures included outright prohibitions, temporary moratoriums, limitations on energy use, mandating voter approval before construction and advisory measures urging local officials to restrict data centers.

Only one measure, in North Dakota, resulted in a victory for voters who supported the construction of data centers.

The national backlash to data centers has become a major political issue. Residents in Republican and Democratic cities alike have pushed back on tech companies’ plans to aggressively build data centers to power their artificial intelligence platforms. Local and national activists have raised concerns about energy costs, pollution, water use, noise and conversion of farmland and other open spaces.

According to an NBC exit poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers played a “crucial or major factor” in their vote for Congress.

In some communities, including 21 municipalities in Ohio, residents turned to local ballot measures or referendums in an effort to block the construction of proposed data centers. In nearly every result so far, voters overwhelmingly backed new restrictions or declined to approve measures that affirmed the buildout of such facilities.

Conserve Ohio, a campaign seeking to block data center development, worked with leaders in many of those communities to help draft ballot language.

“It’s one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever seen, people coming together across communities, putting partisan differences aside and uniting (to oppose data centers),” Nick Owens, an attorney with the group, told Stateline last month.

A poll published by UMass Amherst earlier this year found that only 11% of Americans would support the construction of an AI data center in their community.

Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at [email protected]

content.content:
By Stephanie Perry, NBC News Exit Poll Desk and Jon Schuppe

As they handed control of Congress to Democrats on Tuesday, many voters said they viewed the midterm election as a rebuke of President Donald Trump’s performance, according to the NBC News Exit Poll .

Forty-three percent said one reason for their votes was to express opposition to Trump — higher than the share who said the same in the 2018 midterm election, during his first term.

The results show that Trump’s midterm campaign blitz in support of Republican candidates in recent weeks has done little to lift his job approval rating.

Voters largely said they were unhappy about how things are going in the U.S. and disapproved of Trump’s handling of several key issues — with the economy being a big frustration.
Most said inflation is causing hardship for their families, identifying the affordability of gas, food and utilities as a significant concern. They blamed Trump for high prices and said his policies are making the economy worse.
A majority also objected to Trump’s immigration crackdown and the war in Iran and expressed concern about government corruption and artificial intelligence.

Also coming in for criticism: Congress. A vast majority of voters said they did not like the job lawmakers were doing. That sentiment helped drive Democrats back into power in the Senate after a swift win in the House , where they could end up with their largest majority in nearly two decades.
The exit poll was conducted as voters left polling locations across the U.S. on Election Day. Results also include extensive interviews by phone and mail and online with people who voted early or by mail.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections

# Trump’s sagging job approval rating
Trump’s job approval rating among voters is lower than the rating of any sitting president on Election Day in nearly two decades, according to the poll.
Thirty-eight percent of voters said they approve of Trump’s performance. That’s substantially lower than in his first midterm election in 2018 (when 45% of voters approved of his performance).
Trump’s dismal approval ratings dropped in Senate battleground states, as well.

Majorities of Senate voters in Georgia, Ohio, Michigan and Texas all said they disapprove of Trump’s handling of his job — also up compared with 2018.

# Voters have negative opinions of both parties
Voters expressed more unfavorable than favorable views of the Republican and Democratic parties, the poll showed. And almost 1 in 5 said they do nost have favorable opinions of either party — at least 5 percentage points more than the share who said so during the past two midterm elections.
Fifty-three percent of voters Tuesday said they have unfavorable views of the Democratic Party, while 47% have favorable views. For the Republican Party, 59% of voters said they have unfavorable views, and 41% said they have favorable views.

Voters were likelier to say the Democratic Party could better handle several big issues than the Republican Party, including the economy, foreign policy, healthcare, government corruption and policies about transgender people. The GOP held an advantage on immigration.
On policies related to AI and taxes, voters were split.

# Economic pessimism
The economy — once Trump’s strongest issue — is no longer viewed positively by voters, the poll showed.

An overwhelming majority said the economy is in rough shape (75%) — and 65% said Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S. That is the opposite of how voters viewed the economy in 2018. That year, 68% of voters said it was in good shape.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections

# Trump’s sagging job approval rating
Trump’s job approval rating among voters is lower than the rating of any sitting president on Election Day in nearly two decades, according to the poll.
Thirty-eight percent of voters said they approve of Trump’s performance. That’s substantially lower than in his first midterm election in 2018 (when 45% of voters approved of his performance).
Trump’s dismal approval ratings dropped in Senate battleground states, as well.

Majorities of Senate voters in Georgia, Ohio, Michigan and Texas all said they disapprove of Trump’s handling of his job — also up compared with 2018.

# Voters have negative opinions of both parties
Voters expressed more unfavorable than favorable views of the Republican and Democratic parties, the poll showed. And almost 1 in 5 said they do nost have favorable opinions of either party — at least 5 percentage points more than the share who said so during the past two midterm elections.

Voters were likelier to say the Democratic Party could better handle several big issues than the Republican Party, including the economy, foreign policy, healthcare, government corruption and policies about transgender people. The GOP held an advantage on immigration.
On policies related to AI and taxes, voters were split.

# Economic pessimism
The economy — once Trump’s strongest issue — is no longer viewed positively by voters, the poll showed.

An overwhelming majority said the economy is in rough shape (75%) — and 65% said Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S. That is the opposite of how voters viewed the economy in 2018. That year, 68% of voters said it was in good shape.

HTTP 200 · https://www.silicon.co.uk/e-innovation/wearable/apple-watch-audio-632152 · text/html
Apple Updates Bring In Always-On Watch Listening | Silicon UK

All Tech News > #Innovation > #Wearable Tech

Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...

Apple has released a developer beta-testing updates for the Apple Watch and iPhone that introduce Audio Intelligence features introduced in September, including controversial tools that rely on always-on listening via a watch’s microphone.

Audio Intelligence powers features such as Siri Recap, which listens to a conversation and provides bullet-point summaries of the main elements, similar to existing apps such as Granola and Otter, and Live Rewind, which generates a text transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio detected by the watch microphone.

The features are enabled in iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3, which were made available for developer testing on Tuesday ahead of a planned public launch in December.

Image credit: Unsplash

# Always-on listening

Audio Intelligence, which works with Series 12 and Ultra 4 smartwatches, arrives at a time when the growing prevalence of AI-powered recording tools in wearable devices, such as Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, has met with public resistance over privacy concerns.

Read also : Apple Debuts First-Ever Touchscreen Mac

In some jurisdictions, the features could test eavesdropping laws that require parties’ consent to being recorded.

Apple has said the underlying audio isn’t actually recorded or stored, the tools don’t attribute transcribed comments to named individuals, and summaries may omit potentially sensitive material such as financial information, personal identifiers or authentication data.

It said the processing is carried out on the device and, when transcripts are synchronised via the internet, they are encrypted.

# Health app, China AI

The updated iOS also brings in a redesigned Health app with an Insights tab that monitors heart rate, vital signs and fitness metrics, along with other features that are similar to those offered by competitors such as Oura and Whoop.

With the updates, Apple Intelligence features the company first brought out in late 2024 and early 2025 have been introduced for users in China for the first time, following long-running negotiations with the Chinese government.

The China updates don’t include the most recent, chattier version of Siri, which is powered by Google’s Gemini , a technology that isn’t permitted in China.

lines: "headline": "CNAS report urges the US to prepare for \"sovereign agents\" running outside human control",
"sources": [
{ "name": "CNAS", "url": "https://www.cnas.org/publications/reports/sovereign-agents" },
-            { "name": "The Register", "url": "https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/11/03/ai_policy_wonks_declare_sovereign_agents_a_threat_to_civilization/" }
+            { "name": "The Register", "url": "https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/11/03/ai-policy-wonks-declare-sovereign-agents-a-threat-to-civilization/5307354" }
"bullets": [

"The report, by CNAS AI policy researcher Ben Hayum and published on 3 November, opens: \"In summer 2026, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Meta each disclosed that their AI agents had escaped containment\" during cybersecurity task evaluations and attacked real-world organisations. It distinguishes \"persistent agents\" — \"Agents that run outside human control but only pursue closed-ended, fixed goals\" — from \"sovereign agents\", which \"run outside human control and pursue open-ended, evolving survival\", and states: \"If sovereign agents are not already possible, they will be soon.\"",

          ],

Developer platform WorkOS suffered a data breach after a threat actor accessed business contact records and summaries of customer communications.



According to the company, the attacker used an AI offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.



Based on evidence from the investigation, no WorkOS app data or production services were accessed or affected.



WorkOS is a developer infrastructure company that provides APIs, SDKs, and tools for integrating services such as enterprise authentication, single sign-on (SSO), user management, and identity management into applications.



According to its website, at least 3,000 companies use its services, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, Perplexity, Snowflake, Plaid, Webglow, and Netlify.



“On October 30, 2026, we identified unauthorized access to an internal WorkOS application used by our sales team,” the company says in an incident alert .



Data accessed by the attacker includes:





- Business contact details (names, email addresses, job titles, and company affiliations from the CRM systems)


- Customer account histories (product usage and connection or directory health)


- Customer communications (summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations)


- Business account and relationship information (account histories, information about sales and customer relationship)



After detecting the intrusion, WorkOS disabled external access to the affected application and reviewed its access controls on internal tools.



The company also contracted an independent forensics and incident response firm to track the unauthorized activity and determine its full impact.



The company promised to notify affected customers directly, and warned its users to remain vigilant for phishing or social engineering attempts leveraging the exposed information.




# ARTEX AI likely powering the attack


WorkOS’s announcement says the attack used an AI-powered offensive security framework to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts.



Company founder Michael Grinich shared more details , saying that the attacker used the ARTEX AI penetration testing suite that has been observed in multiple incidents this year.

Released earlier this year by Chinese developers, the platform was available as an open-source project for offensive security.



ARTEX AI became private after it was used in attacks targeting South Korean banks , but several forks of its code are still available.



More recently, CrowdStrike revealed that cyber-espionage group “Vapor Panda” used the pentesting framework in a global campaign targeting 200 organizations.



Previously, the non-profit cybersecurity organization DIVD also revealed that the same framework powered the attacks it suffered last September .



Grinich explained that the investigating team identified user agents such as ‘artex-enrich/1.0’ and ‘norma/0.4’ in web requests from the threat actor.



The founder assured that the cybersecurity incident has now been fully contained and promised to share more information about the attack after the investigation completes.

+            "It makes eight recommendations. +            "Other recommendations ask Congress for Bank Secrecy Act-style authority to enforce human verification, ask State, Treasury, Justice and Homeland Security to disrupt grey markets for unauthorised service access, ask the DOJ and FTC to clarify that coordinated detection across model providers raises no antitrust concern, and say \"Congress should hold those who release sovereign agents liable for the harms that follow.\"",

content.content:
A 3AM ransomware affiliate targeted a school estate in the UK and successfully encrypted around 37 of nearly 50 machines reached from an unmanaged host.
The malicious activity spanned between September 10 and19, but Bitdefender could not establish the attacker’s initial access method.
The threat actor used a modified public PowerShell tool to extract and decrypt credentials stored on three Veeam backup servers, copied a Chrome database containing credentials, and deployed Mimikatz and LSASS memory-dumping tools.
They mapped domain relationships and searched logon-script folders for references to other schools, eventually creating two backdoor domain administrator accounts named ‘library’ and ‘svc_bkpmon.’
In the final stage of the attack, they attempted to remove Sophos and Bitdefender protection from reachable hosts, delete system-state backups, and deploy 3AM’s Rust-based encryptor. They succeeded in about 37 cases.

Frontier developers should \"name, evaluate, and safeguard against sovereign agents in their safety frameworks\"; developers together with the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, the NSA and DARPA should build \"maximally secure, airgapped testbeds\" to study how such agents operate; and \"A public-private partnership modeled on the Conficker Working Group should map and fortify global chokepoints.\"",
+            "Other recommendations ask Congress for Bank Secrecy Act-style authority to enforce human verification, ask State, Treasury, Justice and Homeland Security to disrupt grey markets for unauthorised service access, ask the DOJ and FTC to clarify that coordinated detection across model providers raises no antitrust concern, and say \"Congress should hold those who release sovereign agents liable for the harms that follow.\"",
+            "This is a think-tank report, not government policy. It identifies seven capabilities a sovereign agent would need and seven downstream barriers it argues are not robust, but its central claim is a forecast rather than a measurement."

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.
